title: Git Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Git lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Meet local version history
entries.summary: Version control records changes over time. Git can work on your own computer without a hosting service.
notes: Git and GitHub are different tools: local Git does not require a GitHub account.

entries.name: Start a practice repository
entries.summary: A repository is a project whose history Git tracks. Initialise only a new practice directory for this lesson.

example.code:
mkdir learning-git
cd learning-git
git init

notes: Do not initialise or change an unrelated system folder.

entries.name: Inspect the working tree
entries.summary: The working tree is the set of files you edit. status tells you what is new, changed or ready for a commit.

example.code:
printf "My first note
" > note.txt
git status

notes: Untracked files are not included in a commit unless you add them.

entries.name: Stage the intended changes
entries.summary: The staging area holds the changes you intend to put in the next commit. Add only the files you mean to include.
notes: git add takes the current file content; later edits need another add if they belong in the commit.

entries.name: Make a local commit
entries.summary: A commit records the staged snapshot with a message. Git needs a name and email label, which are part of the commit metadata.

example.code:
git config user.name "Practice Learner"
git config user.email "learner@example.test"
git commit -m "Add first practice note"

notes: Real published commits expose their author metadata; do not use personal details carelessly.

entries.name: Read a difference
entries.summary: A diff shows how current content differs from another version. Review it before saving the next version.

example.code:
printf "A second line
" >> note.txt
git diff

notes: An empty unstaged diff does not prove there are no staged changes.

entries.name: Read the history
entries.summary: The log lists commits. The short view helps you see their order and messages without opening each snapshot.
notes: Commit IDs depend on repository content and metadata; your IDs will differ from another learner's.

entries.name: Try an idea on a branch
entries.summary: A branch is a movable name pointing to a line of commits. It lets you work on a change without immediately adding it to another branch.
notes: A new branch is not a separate full copy of all files on disk.

entries.name: Understand merging
entries.summary: A merge joins histories. If two branches change the same lines differently, Git may need a person to choose the result.

example.code:
git log --oneline --all --graph
# Read the graph before deciding what to merge.

notes: Review and commit or safely save your work before changing branches or merging.

entries.name: Ignore generated files
entries.summary: A .gitignore file lists patterns Git should ignore when files are not already tracked. It is useful for temporary output.
notes: Ignoring a file does not remove it from earlier commits or erase a leaked secret.

entries.name: Inspect remotes
entries.summary: A remote is a named address for another repository. Viewing remotes does not upload or download commits.
notes: Do not paste secret tokens into remote URLs.

entries.name: Share a clear change
entries.summary: A good shared change has a purpose, a reviewed difference and a short explanation of checks. A hosting service can review it separately from local Git.

example.code:
Purpose: add club meeting time
Review: only the intended note changed
Check: read the note and verify the time
Message: Add club meeting time

notes: Do not upload private files or secrets while practising collaboration.
